newsitem.title: UK: Euro Crude Outlook - Tight with Iraq in distance.
newsitem.headline: Euro Crude Outlook - Tight with Iraq in distance.

text.p: European oil traders look ready to put the image of a flood of Iraqi crude to the back of their minds this week and focus instead on a tight short-term market.

"People have been eating and breathing Iraq for weeks, but now they've taken a step back and have realised that it's still some way off...and in the meantime the market is by no means well-supplied," said one trader.
A hurricane in the United States, rebel attacks in Colombia and technical hitches in the North Sea forced oil companies to shut-in production last week, stoking the Atlantic basin market.

In the North Sea, an output cut of 60,000 barrel per day at the Nelson field due to a fault in the gas dehydration system, has already forced the deferral of two Forties cargoes and could lead to further disruptions to loadings, traders said.
Strength at the front end of the market pulled the August/September Brent spread firmly into backwardation, to a high of +19 cents.
"I guess it will stay firm for another week, there are still some shorts to cover,' said one trader.
Some sellers said they were eyeing more transatlantic sales after a trader sold one million barrels of Brent last week into the U.S. Gulf, despite a narrow arbitrage on paper.
But other traders were sceptical about last week's gains, arguing that talk of arbitrage sales was simply an effort to hype bullish sentiment to lift profits on swaps positions.

"The fundamentals just aren't there for a big jump in the market. It's manipulation linked to whatever positions these guys have got...but that doesn't mean they can't keep it strong for a while if they need to," said one North Sea trader.

A July Brent cargo traded 10 cents weaker at September Brent -5 cents on Friday but strong demand for August barrels saw all five Brent cargoes nominated loading dates kept before the five o'clock deadline.

In the Mediterranean, the sour crude market is expected to remain firm, with many buyers simply unable to hold out for bargain prices when Iraqi exports resume next month. Buyers have already bought up all July-loading Russian Urals cargoes, traders said.
"Longer term people are waiting for the collapse of sour grades," said one local refiner. "But the Urals market is short-term and no-one is thinking about late August barrels yet."
In West Africa, good demand from all regions could see the entire August loading programme cleared out by the end of this week.

Forcados and Brass River were swept clean by last Friday and Bonny barrels were available only in the third decade, helping values to firm. The only cloud on the horizon is Iraq, but for now supply tightness persists.
"The return of Iraqi barrels will affect West African ultimately but not in the short term. We're pretty balanced right now," said one trader.

Exports of Iraqi crude under the United Nations oil-for-food deal aren't expected until August but could reach a heavy 1.5 million barrels per day when they do come if Baghdad is to reach its $1-billion revenue target by early September. --Rosalind Russell, Sean Maguire, London +44 171 542 5387
